festivals.name: Ugadi
festivals.description: Homes are decorated with mango leaves and families share ugadi pachadi, whose contrasting flavours symbolise the experiences of life.
festivals.story: Ugadi welcomes the New Year in Telugu and Kannada traditions at the beginning of Chaitra. It is a time for fresh beginnings, spring produce and family visits. Practices differ between Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka: a shared calendar occasion does not mean an identical meal or ceremony everywhere. Household observances are central, while temples and community associations may organise programmes that visitors can attend.
rituals: Decorating entrances and making floor designs
Prayers and listening to the new year’s almanac where locally observed
Sharing foods that combine contrasting tastes
festivals.food: Ugadi pachadi in Telugu households and neem with jaggery in Karnataka express life’s contrasting experiences. Festive sweets vary by region and family.
festivals.dress: Saris, kurtas and other festive clothes are common. Follow the dress guidance of any temple you visit.
tips: Ask your host which local customs they follow; avoid treating one regional tradition as universal.
Arrange a community visit in advance, since a public holiday does not imply open access to homes.
places: A base for Kannada Ugadi observances; confirm individual temple and community programmes.

festivals.name: Sankranti
festivals.description: Rangoli, decorated cattle and family gatherings mark the harvest season.
festivals.story: This guide focuses on Andhra Pradesh’s Sankranti season, when farming families mark the harvest and welcome relatives home. The celebration unfolds across days with distinct names and customs, including Bhogi and Kanuma. The Godavari region is particularly associated with these gatherings. Related midwinter festivals elsewhere in India have their own identities; the Andhra programme should not be assumed to match those of Gujarat or Tamil Nadu.
rituals: Bhogi gatherings at the beginning of the festive period
Decorative muggu floor patterns outside homes
Kanuma observances recognising cattle and agricultural life
festivals.food: Families prepare regional sweets and celebratory meals. Ask what is being served locally instead of expecting a fixed statewide menu.
festivals.dress: Festive saris and traditional clothing are common, alongside everyday dress. Wear practical shoes for village paths.
tips: Choose a hosted village experience or announced public programme; private courtyards are not visitor attractions.
Check the date and location of each day’s activity separately, allowing time for holiday traffic.
places: Gateway to Konaseema celebrations; town-centre marker, not a specific event entrance.

festivals.name: Dree
festivals.description: The Apatani community gathers for agricultural rituals, songs and dances, offering prayers for a healthy crop.
festivals.story: Dree belongs to the Apatani community of Arunachal Pradesh’s Ziro Valley. Its meaning is closely connected to wet-rice cultivation and the wellbeing of people, crops and livestock. Ceremonies seek protection from pests and illness and blessings for fertile fields. Understanding this agricultural relationship helps visitors see Dree as a living community observance, rather than simply a stage performance. Public celebrations and village rites may offer different levels of access.
rituals: Prayers connected with crop protection and wellbeing
Community gatherings during the agricultural festival
Public cultural presentations where announced
festivals.food: Food is shared according to the host community’s arrangements. Ask about ingredients and whether a meal is an invitation or a commercial service.
festivals.dress: Apatani textiles are part of community identity. Visitors can wear comfortable clothing without imitating ceremonial dress.
tips: Use a local host to understand which ceremonies welcome visitors and which are private.
Ask before photographing rituals or people, and keep to paths around working rice fields.
places: Base for Apatani communities in Ziro Valley; confirm the specific celebration ground.

festivals.name: Losar
festivals.description: Monpa communities welcome the new year with monastery prayers, family visits and traditional food.
festivals.story: Losar is a New Year celebration within Tibetan Buddhist cultural traditions. In Tawang it is especially important to Monpa communities; it is also observed in Sikkim and other Himalayan regions. Religious prayers, family reunions and meals accompany hopes for a fortunate year. Local calendars and customs differ, so this guide does not assign one universal date or programme. Tawang’s Torgya monastery festival is a separate occasion and should not be confused with Losar.
rituals: New Year prayers at home and religious venues
Visits and reunions with relatives
Sharing festive meals and greetings
festivals.food: Traditional feasts form part of the celebration. Regional foods and household recipes differ; ask hosts what their dishes signify.
festivals.dress: Wear modest layers for monastery visits. Community ceremonial clothing is meaningful rather than a required visitor costume.
tips: Confirm the community’s own calendar before arranging travel, especially when comparing Himalayan destinations.
Ask separately about monastery access and household invitations; a family celebration may not offer a public performance.
places: Monpa cultural centre; visitor programmes and religious schedules vary.

festivals.name: Bohag Bihu
festivals.description: Also called Rongali Bihu, this spring celebration welcomes the Assamese New Year with Bihu dance, music and festive meals.
festivals.story: Bohag, or Rongali, Bihu marks the Assamese New Year and the arrival of the agricultural spring. It is distinct from Magh Bihu after the harvest and Kati Bihu later in the farming cycle.
rituals: Bihu songs and dancing
Husori group performances
Family visits and exchanges of gamosa cloths
festivals.food: Pitha and laru are familiar festive foods; recipes differ between communities.
festivals.dress: Mekhela chador and gamosa are associated with Assamese celebrations.
tips: Seek a publicly advertised performance if you are visiting independently.
Ask before entering a household celebration.
places: Public Bihu stages and cultural programmes.

festivals.name: Magh Bihu
festivals.description: Community feasts and ceremonial meji bonfires celebrate the end of the harvest season.
festivals.story: Magh Bihu, also called Bhogali Bihu, celebrates the Assamese harvest season with an emphasis on food and community. Uruka, the preceding evening, is a time for shared meals. Temporary gathering structures and the meji bonfire are familiar features, although practices vary across Assam. It is distinct from springtime Bohag Bihu and the more restrained Kati Bihu: planning around the right Bihu matters if you want to understand its agricultural meaning.
rituals: Uruka meals with family and neighbours
Building temporary gathering structures
Meji bonfire observances where locally practised
festivals.food: Pitha is closely associated with the festival; preparations include different rice-based snacks and sweets. A host can explain local varieties and ingredients.
festivals.dress: Assamese textiles may be worn at gatherings. Everyday respectful clothing is appropriate unless an organiser advises otherwise.
tips: Arrange access through a host instead of assuming a village feast is open to every passer-by.
Observe bonfires from a safe distance and follow local organisers’ instructions around temporary structures.
places: Town and surrounding communities; each Uruka gathering has its own arrangements.

festivals.name: Chhath Puja
festivals.description: Devotees offer prayers to the setting and rising sun at rivers and ponds, with fasting and carefully prepared offerings.
festivals.story: Chhath is an observance of gratitude to the sun and Chhathi Maiya. It is especially associated with Bihar and neighbouring regions, and is also observed by communities far from their home states.
rituals: Fasting and carefully prepared offerings
Prayers to the setting sun
Prayers at sunrise near water
festivals.food: Thekua and fruit are among the offerings; preparation follows household religious practices.
festivals.dress: Dress respectfully and keep worship areas clear.
tips: Do not interrupt fasting devotees or step across offerings.
Stay behind waterside barriers; ask before close-up photographs.
places: Designated river ghats; access arrangements change by year.

practical.duration: Four days, with offerings to the setting and rising sun on different stages of the observance.
practical.suggestedVisit: 1–2 days around a locally confirmed evening and following dawn observance.
practical.cost: Budget for lodging, local travel and meals. The tourism listing indicates no ticket for the festival; this does not make transport, private access or hosted services free.
practical.booking: Confirm which ghat welcomes observers and its access rules. Arrange early-morning transport and a meeting point away from the water; follow local crowd-control instructions.

festivals.name: Sonepur Mela
festivals.description: Around Kartik Purnima, pilgrims, performers and traders gather at this historic riverside fair.
festivals.story: Sonepur Mela brings together pilgrimage, trade and cultural programmes near the confluence of the Ganga and Gandak in Bihar. Its opening is associated with Kartik Purnima, when devotees visit the rivers and Harihar Nath Temple. The fair is historically known for livestock trading, but visitors can also explore crafts, performances and the atmosphere of a large regional gathering. Historic descriptions of animal sales should not be treated as a current programme or an invitation to buy wildlife.
rituals: Kartik Purnima pilgrimage and temple prayers
Browsing market stalls and regional crafts
Announced music and cultural performances
festivals.food: Fairground vendors offer snacks and meals. Choose freshly prepared food and ask about ingredients; no single dish defines the whole mela.
festivals.dress: Respectful everyday clothing and comfortable footwear suit the combination of religious visits and long walks.
tips: Check the current fairground plan and performance schedule before visiting.
Use designated riverside routes and keep photography away from people bathing or worshipping.
places: Town near the river confluence; current fair entrances must be checked locally.

festivals.name: Bastar Dussehra
festivals.description: A long cycle of rituals honours Goddess Danteshwari, bringing together local communities, ceremonial chariots and regional deities.
festivals.story: Bastar Dussehra is a long cycle of observances centred on Danteshwari and the deity traditions of Bastar. Unlike many other Dussehra celebrations, it does not centre on burning an effigy of Ravana. Village deities and their representatives gather, while chariot-making connects skilled craft, faith and collective participation. The cycle extends far beyond the main procession days, so choosing a particular ritual is more useful than assuming there is one short festival weekend.
rituals: Pat Jatra associated with wood for the chariot
Crafting the ceremonial wooden chariot
Gatherings of deities and chariot processions
festivals.food: Explore regional food through public vendors or a local host. Ritual offerings and private community meals follow their own rules.
festivals.dress: Dress respectfully and keep hands free in crowds. Community regalia and deity objects should never be handled without permission.
tips: Choose authorised viewing areas and keep clear of chariot ropes and procession routes.
Ask a local guide to explain the specific stage you are seeing rather than applying another region’s Dussehra story.
places: Main town associated with Bastar Dussehra; procession routes are programme-dependent.

festivals.name: Hareli
festivals.description: Farming communities honour agricultural tools and celebrate the green season with local games and traditions.
festivals.story: Hareli is associated with the greenery of the monsoon and Chhattisgarh’s agricultural life. Village celebrations recognise the work of farming and the season’s hopes for growth. Gedi, the practice of walking on bamboo stilts, is a well-known cultural feature in parts of the state. On Hareli Amavasya, Bastar also observes Pat Jatra within its longer Dussehra cycle; that specific rite should be distinguished from the broader household and village festival.
rituals: Respecting agricultural tools and farming work
Village gatherings marking the monsoon season
Gedi displays where locally organised
festivals.food: Household and village meals vary. Ask your host about local preparations rather than expecting a standard festival menu.
festivals.dress: Comfortable everyday clothing suits public gatherings. Village participants may use regional festive dress.
tips: Confirm that a village gathering welcomes visitors and ask before entering farms or courtyards.
Watch stilt demonstrations from the space organisers provide; do not handle equipment without an invitation.
places: A planning base for announced cultural programmes and nearby village visits.
sources: Chhattisgarh district administration: Culture and heritage
Ministry of Tourism: Bastar heritage trail and Pat Jatra

festivals.name: Carnival
festivals.description: Colourful floats, music and dancing fill the streets in the days leading up to Lent.
festivals.story: Goa’s Carnival, often written Carnaval, is a public celebration with processions, music, costumes and decorated floats. Its history is linked to the pre-Lenten carnival tradition, with a distinctive Goan expression today. Parades in different towns form separate programmes rather than one continuously moving event. The figure of King Momo is associated with the festivities. Carnival is distinct from Shigmo, another major Goan celebration with its own seasonal and cultural roots.
rituals: Decorated float parades
Music and dance along announced routes
Costume presentations and community entertainment
festivals.food: Food vendors and nearby restaurants offer varied Goan dishes. Ask about seafood, meat and vegetarian ingredients rather than assuming a uniform carnival menu.
festivals.dress: Costumes belong to participating groups; spectators can wear light, comfortable clothes and walking shoes.
tips: Use the published town-by-town route and arrival information to choose a viewing point.
Respect barriers and give floats and performers room; arrange your return journey before road closures begin.
places: One of the parade cities; confirm the current route and viewing arrangements.

festivals.name: Shigmo
festivals.description: Folk dances, processions and elaborate floats bring Goan spring traditions into public celebrations.
festivals.story: Shigmo is a Goan spring celebration rooted in local community and religious traditions. Music, folk dance and processions carry these traditions into public space. Organised town parades include cultural presentations and floats, while village observances have their own character and timing. Shigmo is not another name for Carnival: learning which event is scheduled will help you understand the performances and avoid travelling for the wrong programme.
rituals: Folk music and dance presentations
Community processions and local observances
Decorated floats at organised Shigmotsav parades
festivals.food: Try regional food from public stalls or restaurants. Household festive dishes vary, and religious spaces may have their own food restrictions.
festivals.dress: Performers wear costumes suited to their tradition. Visitors need comfortable clothing rather than ceremonial dress.
tips: Check the parade schedule for the particular town you want to visit; dates differ across Goa.
Ask before close-up photographs and stay out of performance formations, especially when instruments or large floats are moving.
places: A base for Goan cultural traditions; confirm announced parade and village programmes.
sources: Goa Tourism: Faith and heritage celebrations

festivals.name: Navratri
festivals.description: Nine nights of devotion to the goddess are celebrated with circular garba dancing and dandiya raas.
festivals.story: Navratri honours the goddess over nine nights. Gujarat's garba circles and dandiya gatherings are especially well known, while other regions have distinct devotional and artistic traditions. This guide focuses on the autumn celebration.
rituals: Garba and dandiya raas
Prayers and household observances
Community gatherings over successive evenings
festivals.food: Fasting and festive menus differ. Ask hosts about the customs of the event you attend.
festivals.dress: Chaniya cholis and kediyu outfits are associated with Gujarati celebrations; comfortable footwear and freedom of movement matter.
tips: Join dancing only where visitors are welcome; follow the direction of the circle.
Check passes and entry rules for each venue.
places: Large organised dance gatherings; passes vary.

practical.duration: Nine nights; each garba venue may operate a different programme.
practical.suggestedVisit: 2–3 evenings in one city, leaving daytime for rest and sightseeing.
practical.cost: Community and commercial events have different admission arrangements. Confirm single-night versus season passes, inclusions and refund terms with the venue.
practical.booking: Choose a named garba venue and confirm admission, dress expectations, start times and transport home. A general tourism listing does not establish entry conditions at every venue.

festivals.name: Uttarayan
festivals.description: Rooftops fill with kite flyers during Makar Sankranti, with festive food and colourful skies.
festivals.story: Uttarayan is closely associated with kite flying across Gujarat around Makar Sankranti. Rooftops and open grounds become social spaces where families and friends watch the sky and share food. Ahmedabad’s organised International Kite Festival adds a public showcase of imaginative kites and visiting flyers. That scheduled event is related to, but not identical with, everyday neighbourhood celebrations; its venue and dates need separate confirmation.
rituals: Kite flying and watching from open spaces
Neighbourhood and family gatherings
Demonstrations at the organised International Kite Festival
festivals.food: Seasonal food is part of gatherings, but menus vary by household. Ask a local host about their favourite winter dishes and dietary ingredients.
festivals.dress: Wear comfortable clothes, sun protection and secure footwear. Rooftop access is not a reason to approach unprotected edges.
tips: Choose a public viewing ground or an explicitly hosted rooftop visit.
Avoid hazardous kite string and never retrieve kites near traffic or power lines; follow local organiser guidance.
places: Public kite-festival programmes and neighbourhood celebrations; verify the current venue.

festivals.name: Teej
festivals.description: Songs, swings and gatherings celebrate the arrival of the monsoon and the traditions of Teej.
festivals.story: This guide focuses on Haryana’s monsoon Teej traditions. The festival connects devotion to Parvati and Shiva with family relationships and the relief brought by seasonal rain. Women’s gatherings, songs, dance, mehendi and swings are familiar expressions of the occasion. Teej is observed in several regions and includes differently named observances; a public celebration in Haryana need not share the ritual calendar or procession format of Jaipur.
rituals: Women’s songs and dance gatherings
Mehendi and decorated swings
Prayers and family observances, including fasting for some participants
festivals.food: Festive foods and sweets accompany social gatherings, while fasting practices vary. Ask hosts before offering food to someone observing a fast.
festivals.dress: Colourful festive clothing and jewellery are common. Visitors can dress respectfully without copying personal or ceremonial adornment.
tips: Ask before joining a women’s gathering or photographing participants at close range.
Check whether an advertised programme is a public cultural event or a private devotional observance.
places: Haryana cultural setting; identify a publicly announced local celebration before travelling.

festivals.name: Surajkund International Crafts Mela
festivals.description: Artisans and performers gather for a major cultural fair showcasing handicrafts, folk traditions and regional food.
festivals.story: Surajkund International Crafts Mela is an organised fair in Faridabad that brings craftspeople, weavers and performing groups together. Its central purpose is to give artisans a place to demonstrate and sell their work directly. Textiles, pottery and many other craft traditions appear alongside cultural performances. Themes and participating regions change between editions, so an old brochure is useful background but does not guarantee a particular stall or show this year.
rituals: Browsing artisan and handloom stalls
Watching craft demonstrations where offered
Folk performances at the mela’s open-air stages
festivals.food: The fair offers a variety of regional food choices. Check individual vendors for ingredients and dietary needs; no single cuisine represents the event.
festivals.dress: Comfortable walking shoes and weather-appropriate clothing are more useful than formal dress for exploring the large grounds.
tips: Ask makers about materials, technique and care instructions before buying.
Check official ticketing, gate access and the performance schedule; allow time to return to the correct exit.
places: City-centre reference; the mela itself is at Surajkund, with designated gates.

practical.duration: The archived 2026 edition ran 31 January–15 February. That duration does not confirm a future edition.
practical.suggestedVisit: One full day for crafts, food and selected performances; two days for a slower visit.
practical.cost: Ticketed fair: follow Haryana Tourism to the current authorised ticket seller. Future edition prices and concessions are not verified here.
practical.booking: Confirm the edition and date on the ticket page. Budget separately for purchases, meals and travel; the Diwali Mela is a different event.

festivals.name: Kullu Dussehra
festivals.description: Valley deities are brought to Kullu in a gathering centred on Lord Raghunath, with processions and cultural programmes.
festivals.story: Kullu Dussehra brings local deities and their representatives together around Lord Raghunath. A ceremonial chariot journey into Dhalpur forms a central public moment, followed by a wider fair and cultural programme. The gathering expresses relationships between valley communities as well as devotion. Its sequence differs from familiar one-day Dussehra spectacles elsewhere, so the arrival of deities, processions and performances should be planned as distinct experiences.
rituals: Arrival of community deities and their attendants
Lord Raghunath’s ceremonial chariot procession
Cultural performances and fairground gatherings
festivals.food: Explore local food through public stalls and restaurants. Sacred offerings and community meals may have separate arrangements and access rules.
festivals.dress: Layered clothing suits outdoor viewing. Regional caps and textiles are part of local dress, not compulsory visitor attire.
tips: Keep clear of chariot ropes, bearers and deity palanquins even when taking photographs.
Check the current Dhalpur programme and allow extra travel time around procession closures.
places: Dhalpur is associated with the main gathering; confirm current entrances and viewing areas.
sources: Himachal Tourism: Temples and deity traditions

practical.duration: A week-long celebration in Kullu, centred on Dhalpur grounds.
practical.suggestedVisit: 2–3 days to see selected processions and explore Kullu, plus travel time.
practical.cost: Current entry or seating charges are not verified here. Set aside separate budgets for accommodation, local travel and meals.
practical.booking: Check the official procession programme before choosing dates. Ask your accommodation about access and pickup points during road restrictions.

festivals.name: Mandi Shivratri
festivals.description: Local deities, devotees and performers gather for a celebration associated with Maha Shivratri.
festivals.story: Mandi Shivratri combines religious observances with a major gathering of local deities, processions and cultural events. Bhootnath Temple and the presence of Madho Rai are important within its ceremonial setting. The fair gives visitors an opportunity to understand how village deity traditions relate to the town. Evening performances, exhibitions and the religious sequence are different parts of the occasion; they may operate on separate schedules.
rituals: Gathering of local deities and their attendants
Religious visits and ceremonial processions
Cultural evenings, exhibitions and public fair activities
festivals.food: Himachali dham is associated with regional celebrations and is mentioned in tourism accounts of the fair. Confirm where meals are offered and how to join.
festivals.dress: Respectful layers suit temple visits and outdoor evenings. Colourful local turbans are part of procession dress.
tips: Give bearers and worshippers priority around temples and processions.
Check the daily programme before choosing between a religious observance and an evening cultural performance.
places: Town-centre reference; official programme identifies procession and fair venues.

festivals.name: Sarhul
festivals.description: Several Adivasi communities honour sacred groves and the flowering sal tree with rituals, music and dancing.
festivals.story: Sarhul welcomes spring among several Adivasi communities in Jharkhand. Sal blossoms are closely associated with the occasion, linking worship and community life to the changing season. Songs, dancing and gatherings express renewal, but names, narratives and ritual details differ between communities. A public city procession offers one way to encounter Sarhul; it should not be treated as a complete representation of every village’s sacred practices.
rituals: Community worship associated with the spring season
Use of sal blossoms in local observances
Songs, dancing and public gatherings
festivals.food: Families prepare celebratory food according to their own traditions. Ask before accepting or photographing offerings, and check ingredients with your host.
festivals.dress: White saris with red borders appear in public celebrations, among other regional clothing. Visitors do not need to adopt community dress.
tips: Ask permission before entering a sacred grove or approaching a ritual area.
Use a local guide or host to identify the community and meaning of the celebration rather than describing all practices as the same.
places: Public processions and nearby community celebrations; access differs by site.

festivals.name: Karam
festivals.description: Community celebrations centre on the Karam tree, with songs and dances expressing hopes for wellbeing and prosperity.
festivals.story: Karam centres on reverence for Karam devta and is observed by several communities in Jharkhand and neighbouring regions. Young people, communal singing and dance are prominent in accounts of the celebration. Its relationship with nature, wellbeing and collective life makes the ritual setting important, not merely the performance. Practices vary, so a host’s explanation of their own observance is more reliable than assuming one statewide sequence.
rituals: Worship associated with Karam devta
Community songs and dance
Gatherings in which young people play an important role
festivals.food: Offerings and shared meals follow local custom. Ask hosts about preparation and participation rather than assuming every gathering has a public feast.
festivals.dress: Regional festive textiles and everyday dress vary by community. Choose respectful clothing and avoid handling ceremonial objects.
tips: Ask which activities are public and where visitors may stand before a ceremony starts.
Seek permission for portraits and recordings, particularly when songs or rituals are not intended as public performances.
places: A base for learning about local Karam traditions; arrange a specific hosted visit.

festivals.name: Mysuru Dasara
festivals.description: An illuminated palace, performances and the celebrated procession make Dasara a signature Mysuru experience.
festivals.story: Mysuru Dasara combines worship of Chamundeshwari with the city's royal and public cultural heritage. Palace illumination and performances build towards the festival's celebrated procession. Specific programmes can have separate tickets.

Classical and folk performances
The ceremonial Dasara procession
festivals.food: Mysore pak is a local sweet to try; it is not exclusive to Dasara.
festivals.dress: Comfortable clothing works for public viewing; follow dress requirements in religious venues.
tips: Verify procession dates and viewing arrangements separately.
Book accommodation early and allow for traffic restrictions.
places: Palace area and announced city programme locations.

festivals.name: Onam
festivals.description: Floral pookalam designs, the onasadya feast and cultural performances celebrate the homecoming of King Mahabali.
festivals.story: Onam celebrates seasonal abundance and the legendary return of King Mahabali. It brings Malayali families and communities together through floral designs, hospitality and performances. Public programmes and household traditions have different schedules.
rituals: Pookalam floral designs
An Onasadya meal served on a banana leaf
Cultural performances and community gatherings

festivals.dress: Kerala kasavu textiles are often worn for celebrations. Comfortable, respectful clothing is suitable for visitors.
tips: Book a public sadya rather than assuming access to a private family meal.
Boat races are separate events: verify their dates independently.
places: Look for announced city cultural programmes.
Community celebrations and public sadya meals.

practical.cost: Restaurant sadya meals, boat-race seating and cultural shows may have separate charges. Current menus and ticket prices are not verified here.
practical.booking: Reserve a sadya sitting with the restaurant and check dietary needs directly. Match any boat race or performance to its own published programme, rather than assuming it coincides with Thiruvonam.

festivals.name: Vishu
festivals.description: The day begins with viewing the auspicious Vishukkani arrangement, followed by gifts and family meals.
festivals.story: Vishu marks an auspicious solar-calendar occasion in Kerala, usually during April. The first sight of the day, Vishukkani, is central: an arrangement of produce, flowers, a mirror and other meaningful objects is prepared with care. Gifts from elders and a shared feast connect the ritual to family life. Household practices and temple observances differ, and Vishu should not be treated as interchangeable with Onam or every other regional New Year.
rituals: Viewing the Vishukkani arrangement on waking
Vishukkaineetam gifts from elders
Family meals and temple visits where observed
festivals.food: Vishu sadya offers a range of Kerala dishes; menus vary. Vishu katta is another regional preparation associated with the occasion.
festivals.dress: Kerala saris and mundu are familiar festive choices. Temple dress requirements may be more specific, so check before visiting.
tips: A household Vishukkani is an intimate family moment: arrange a host’s invitation rather than arriving unannounced.
If booking a festive meal, confirm its menu and service time independently of temple schedules.
places: A Kerala cultural base; confirm the specific temple or hosted family arrangements.

festivals.name: Bhagoria
festivals.description: Bhil and Bhilala communities gather at lively fairs before Holi, with music, dancing and market stalls.
festivals.story: Bhagoria is a series of fairs associated especially with Bhil and Bhilala communities in western Madhya Pradesh. Held around local market days before Holi, the gatherings connect the end of the harvest with music, dance, social visits and trade. Jhabua, Alirajpur, Dhar and Khargone are among the regions associated with it. Reducing Bhagoria to a sensational story about courtship overlooks its agricultural, commercial and community importance.
rituals: Market-day gatherings at local haats
Traditional music and group dancing
Exchange of colour where participants welcome it
festivals.food: Market stalls offer food and seasonal produce. Ask vendors about ingredients; everyday regional cuisine and ritual food are not necessarily the same.
festivals.dress: Bright clothing and silver ornaments appear in community dress. Ask permission for photographs rather than treating participants as exhibits.
tips: Find the local haat calendar, since different towns celebrate on different days.
Ask before applying colour, joining a dance or photographing personal interactions; participation should always be welcome.
places: Base for regional haats; identify the exact market and day locally.

festivals.name: Khajuraho Dance Festival
festivals.description: Indian classical dance traditions are showcased against the backdrop of Khajuraho’s temple heritage.
festivals.story: Khajuraho Dance Festival presents Indian classical dance in the setting of Khajuraho’s monumental heritage. It is a curated arts programme, with named performers and scheduled presentations, rather than a single religious rite shared by all visitors. Different dance traditions bring distinctive movement, music and storytelling. Reading the programme before attending makes it easier to understand what you are watching and to choose performances that interest you.
rituals: Scheduled classical dance recitals
Musical accompaniment and expressive storytelling
Associated cultural activities when included by organisers
festivals.food: Food is part of the wider visitor experience rather than a defining ritual. Plan a meal around performance times and use the designated eating areas.
festivals.dress: Comfortable, respectful evening clothing is suitable for audiences. Performers’ costumes belong to particular dance traditions.
tips: Check the current performance roster, venue and entry arrangements; an earlier edition’s lineup is not a promise.
Keep phones silent and follow rules on flash, filming and movement during a recital; visit the monuments separately if required.

festivals.name: Ganesh Chaturthi
festivals.description: Ganesha idols are welcomed into homes and public pandals, with prayers, modak sweets and immersion processions.
festivals.story: Ganesh Chaturthi welcomes Ganesha into homes and public pandals. Maharashtra's community celebrations combine worship, craftsmanship and collective organisation. Household observances vary in duration, so immersion days are not identical everywhere.
rituals: Installation of Ganesha idols
Aarti and offerings
Visarjan immersion processions
festivals.food: Modak sweets are strongly associated with Ganesha; recipes and offerings vary.
festivals.dress: Respectful, comfortable clothing is suitable; follow temple or pandal instructions.
tips: Use designated viewing areas for processions and immersion.
Allow extra time for queues and temporary road closures.
places: Major public pandals and immersion routes.

practical.cost: Allow for local transport, meals and any guided visits. Current special-access charges are not verified; do not assume a paid tour gives priority darshan.

festivals.name: Gudi Padwa
festivals.description: Families raise decorated gudis outside their homes to welcome the new year.
festivals.story: Gudi Padwa welcomes the Marathi New Year at the beginning of Chaitra. A gudi, raised outside the home, gives the celebration its distinctive visual symbol and expresses auspiciousness and renewal. Household prayers and meals sit alongside public shobhayatra processions in places such as Pune and Mumbai. It shares a seasonal setting with other regional New Year celebrations, but its customs and local programmes deserve their own attention.
rituals: Raising and worshipping a decorated gudi
Making rangoli and decorating entrances
Community shobhayatra processions where announced
festivals.food: Puran poli and shrikhand are familiar festive foods. Neem and jaggery can express acceptance of life’s bitter and sweet experiences; customs vary.
festivals.dress: Saris, kurtas and regional festive clothing are common. Comfortable footwear is useful for public procession viewing.
tips: View household gudis from public space unless invited inside.
Confirm the route and time of the particular shobhayatra, and leave clear space for performers and worshippers.
places: Public processions and household traditions; check neighbourhood-specific schedules.

festivals.name: Yaoshang
festivals.description: A multiday spring celebration combines devotional traditions, local sports and thabal chongba dancing.
festivals.story: Yaoshang is an important spring celebration in Manipur, traditionally extending over several days around the full moon of Phalguna. It is especially associated with Meitei cultural life. Thabal Chongba, in which participants form a circle and dance together, is a recognisable part of the festive season. Community programmes vary, so the festival is best understood through a particular neighbourhood’s arrangements rather than a single assumed statewide timetable.
rituals: Community gatherings over the spring festive period
Thabal Chongba circle dancing
Local cultural activities according to the neighbourhood programme
festivals.food: Explore local food through public vendors or a host. Festival hospitality does not imply that every household meal is open to visitors.
festivals.dress: Participants may wear Manipuri textiles and festive clothes. Ask hosts about appropriate clothing if invited to join an activity.
tips: Obtain the local programme and confirm that visitors may attend the dance gathering.
Join only when invited, follow the group’s lead and ask before photographing people; confirm current local travel arrangements before making plans.
places: Neighbourhood celebrations have separate organisers and access arrangements.

festivals.name: Sangai Festival
festivals.description: A tourism festival presents the state’s dance, crafts, food and cultural traditions.
festivals.story: Sangai Festival is an organised showcase of Manipur’s arts, crafts, cuisine and sporting traditions. It takes its name from the state’s distinctive brow-antlered deer. Past editions have brought performances, handlooms and demonstrations together across several venues, helping visitors encounter the diversity of the state. This is an annual event whose delivery depends on organiser announcements: a historical programme should not be presented as confirmation of a forthcoming edition.
rituals: Announced dance and music performances
Handloom and craft exhibitions
Demonstrations of indigenous games when programmed
festivals.food: Past food programmes have included dishes such as eromba, singju and fish curry. Ingredients vary; ask specifically about fermented fish and vegetarian preparation.
festivals.dress: Comfortable clothing suits exhibition grounds. Performance costumes represent distinct communities rather than one universal Manipuri outfit.
tips: Confirm that the edition is going ahead, then check venues, tickets and local travel arrangements.
Plan transport between venues instead of assuming all activities occur in one fairground; ask makers before photographing their work.
places: Planning base; festival venues may also be outside the city.
sources: Manipur Tourism: Sangai Festival background and past programme

festivals.name: Wangala
festivals.description: Garo communities celebrate the harvest with drumming and dancing, giving thanks to the sun deity.
festivals.story: Wangala is a Garo harvest celebration associated with gratitude to Saljong and the agricultural cycle. Drumming and coordinated dancing are important public expressions of the occasion, especially in the well-known Hundred Drums presentation. Village observances have their own settings and calendars; the organised showcase should not be mistaken for the only form of Wangala. Learning from a Garo host helps connect the performances to their cultural and spiritual meaning.
rituals: Harvest thanksgiving observances
Rhythmic group dancing accompanied by drums
Community gatherings and organised cultural presentations
festivals.food: Garo food and traditional beverages may be offered. Ask about ingredients and alcohol content; accepting a drink is not necessary to appreciate the gathering.
festivals.dress: Community textiles and headpieces carry cultural meaning. Visitors can wear practical clothes and ask before photographing or handling ornaments.
tips: Check the specific village or showcase programme instead of assuming one date applies throughout the Garo Hills.
Keep dance lines and drummers’ space clear, and seek guidance before approaching ritual areas.
places: Base for Garo Hills visits; verify the actual Wangala ground separately.

photo.alt: Drummers and dancers in colourful clothing performing outdoors at Wangala
photo.caption: Wangala at Chibragre, West Garo Hills, November 2021. Historical photograph.
photo.author: Visma kumar

festivals.name: Nongkrem Dance Festival
festivals.description: Khasi ceremonial traditions and dances express thanksgiving and prayers for prosperity.
festivals.story: Nongkrem is a Khasi thanksgiving festival held at Smit, the traditional seat of Hima Khyrim near Shillong. Its ceremonies connect prayers for prosperity and a good harvest with the responsibilities of the Syiem and religious authorities. The public dance is one part of a larger sacred observance, rather than a performance arranged simply for visitors. Women and men have distinct roles, and the ceremonial dress, music and movement carry community meanings. Autumn is a useful planning window, but the organising authorities announce the actual programme.
rituals: Thanksgiving ceremonies associated with the Pomblang observance
Women and men performing ceremonial dances in the courtyard
Traditional instrumental music accompanying the dancers
festivals.food: Look for locally run Khasi food stalls nearby; refreshments for visitors are separate from ceremonial offerings. Ask about ingredients and vegetarian options.
festivals.dress: Dancers wear elaborate Khasi ceremonial textiles and ornaments. Visitors can wear comfortable, respectful everyday clothing.
tips: Stay outside the designated dancing space and ask before photographing ceremonial participants.
Confirm the principal dance day before arranging transport from Shillong; allow time for traffic near Smit.
places: Approximate village centre; follow local directions to the ceremonial courtyard.

festivals.name: Chapchar Kut
festivals.description: A Mizo spring festival with music, traditional dress and dances including the bamboo dance, Cheraw.
festivals.story: Chapchar Kut is a spring celebration rooted in the agricultural rhythm of jhum cultivation. It marks a pause after the demanding work of clearing land, bringing people together through music, dancing and shared festivities. Contemporary public programmes also celebrate Mizo cultural identity, textiles and performance. Aizawl is a useful starting point for a visitor, though local communities hold their own events. The usual spring season should not be treated as a fixed annual date: the announced programme determines when the main gathering takes place.
rituals: Traditional dances and songs performed by community groups
Drum and cymbal accompaniment
Public gatherings showcasing Mizo dress and cultural expression
festivals.food: Bamboo-shoot and leafy vegetable preparations are regional foods to explore. Menus vary by vendor, so ask about meat or fermented ingredients.
festivals.dress: Performers often wear bright Mizo woven clothing and headgear; visitors do not need ceremonial costume.
tips: Check the published Aizawl programme and venue before making bookings.
Watch organised dances from the audience area; join participatory activities only when invited.
places: City centre reference; confirm the announced festival ground.

photo.alt: Dancers stepping between bamboo poles with spectators on the hillside at Vairengte
photo.caption: Chapchar Kut dance in Vairengte, Mizoram. Historical photograph; the filename and recorded date differ, so the capture year is unconfirmed.
photo.author: Anup Rou

festivals.name: Mim Kut
festivals.description: A traditional maize-season observance combines remembrance of departed relatives with community customs.
festivals.story: Mim Kut is one of the traditional seasonal festivals documented by Mizoram Tourism, which describes it as the Maize Festival. It belongs to the agricultural and cultural heritage of Mizo communities, with singing, dancing and communal enjoyment associated with the celebration. Accounts of older practices and present-day gatherings can differ, so a historical description should not be assumed to describe every household today. Unlike a large annual ticketed event, a local observance may have no advertised visitor programme. Ask a community host what is being celebrated and which activities welcome guests.
rituals: Community songs and dances where locally organised
Gatherings connected with the seasonal harvest
Sharing food according to the host community’s customs
festivals.food: Harvest foods and local meals vary between communities. Historical accounts mention rice beer, but visitors should not assume it is served or required.
festivals.dress: Woven Mizo clothing may feature in cultural programmes. Everyday respectful dress is appropriate unless organisers advise otherwise.
tips: Confirm that a public gathering is taking place before planning travel around it.
Ask permission before entering family gatherings or photographing participants.
places: Planning base for local cultural information; not a guaranteed public festival venue.

festivals.name: Hornbill Festival
festivals.description: Naga communities share performances, crafts, food and traditions at a major annual cultural gathering.
festivals.story: Organised as a cultural showcase since 2000, Hornbill brings together different Naga communities. It offers performances, crafts and food alongside contemporary events. The shared programme does not replace each community's own festivals or distinct traditions.
rituals: Cultural presentations at Kisama
Craft and textile demonstrations
Music and community food stalls
festivals.food: Stalls offer different Naga cuisines. Ask vendors about ingredients, spice levels and vegetarian options.
festivals.dress: Community textiles and ornaments have specific meanings; ask before borrowing, handling or photographing them closely.
tips: Check the current official programme and visitor requirements before booking.
Ask performers before portraits, and keep performance areas clear.
places: Main cultural showcase near Kohima; programme and access are organiser-dependent.

practical.duration: A ten-day festival; daily activities and individual performances vary.
practical.suggestedVisit: 2–3 festival days, with additional time for journeys to and from Kisama.
practical.cost: Current admission, concert and activity prices are not verified here. Ask which activities are covered by each ticket before buying.
practical.booking: Use Nagaland Tourism for the current programme and ticket information. Arrange accommodation and transfers around the days you choose.

photo.caption: Hornbill Festival at Kisama, 2024. Historical photograph.

festivals.name: Moatsu
festivals.description: After sowing, Ao communities celebrate with songs, dances and communal gatherings.
festivals.story: Moatsu is an Ao Naga festival associated with community bonding after agricultural work. The Ministry of Tourism describes a three-day celebration in May, bringing people together through shared festivities. Its importance lies in the relationships renewed among neighbours and families, alongside cultural expression. Mokokchung and surrounding Ao villages provide the relevant geographical context, but an announced public event and a village’s own observance may have different arrangements. Treat the general season as an introduction and seek the host community’s programme before making a special journey.
rituals: Community gatherings and shared celebrations
Traditional music and dance in organised programmes
Hospitality that renews relationships among participants
festivals.food: Food is arranged by the host community; ask what is included before accepting a meal, particularly if you avoid meat or particular ingredients.
festivals.dress: Ao shawls and traditional clothing may be worn by participants. Ceremonial garments have meanings that a local guide can explain.
tips: Contact a local host to identify public events in the Mokokchung area.
Ask before photographing people or joining a group meal; private hospitality is by invitation.
places: Town centre reference for Ao community celebrations in the surrounding area.

festivals.name: Rath Yatra
festivals.description: The deities Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra travel in monumental wooden chariots through Puri.
festivals.story: Puri's Rath Yatra brings Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra into a public chariot procession. The journey forms part of a larger cycle of observances, including the return journey, which must be checked separately.
rituals: Wooden chariot construction
The outward chariot procession
Later return observances
festivals.food: Mahaprasad is associated with Jagannath traditions; seek guidance on authorised distribution.
festivals.dress: Wear respectful clothing and practical footwear for long periods outdoors.
tips: Use authorised viewing arrangements rather than entering dense chariot crowds.
Temple entry restrictions differ from access to the public procession.
places: Grand Road procession corridor; access follows local arrangements.

practical.duration: The Puri tourism guide describes a nine-day festival cycle, including the outward and return journeys. Individual rituals have separate timings.
practical.suggestedVisit: 2–3 days around one chosen procession or ritual; seeing the full cycle requires a longer stay.
practical.cost: Accommodation, transport and any arranged viewing have separate costs. No verified universal visitor admission price or guaranteed viewing package is supplied here.
practical.booking: Choose the outward or return journey deliberately and confirm its date. Ask about pedestrian access, road restrictions and the actual viewing location before booking a guide or room.

photo.alt: Three brightly decorated festival chariots lit at night with visitors in front
photo.caption: Rath Yatra chariots near Gundicha Temple in Puri, July 2011. Historical photograph.
photo.author: Zephyrmaten

festivals.name: Raja Parba
festivals.description: A celebration associated with the earth’s fertility, featuring swings, pitha and a pause in agricultural work.
festivals.story: Raja Parba celebrates womanhood and the renewal of the earth at the approach of the monsoon in Odisha. The three-day observance symbolically gives Mother Earth rest, with agricultural work traditionally paused. Swings, games, new clothes and festive food are prominent parts of the celebration, particularly for girls and women. It is both a household occasion and a community festival; public Raja events can provide a welcoming introduction for visitors. Customs vary across Odisha, and the symbolism is best understood through the voices of the people who practise it.
rituals: Decorated swings and traditional games
A symbolic pause in agricultural work
Family and community gatherings celebrating seasonal renewal
festivals.food: Pitha and other festive treats are a good starting point for exploring Odia food. Ask vendors about ingredients and preparation rather than assuming a single standard menu.
festivals.dress: New festive clothing is common; visitors can choose light, comfortable clothing suitable for outdoor gatherings.
tips: Look for announced public Raja programmes in Bhubaneswar rather than entering private celebrations.
Ask permission before using a community swing and wait for organisers to supervise children.
places: City centre reference; public Raja venues vary by edition.
sources: Odisha Tourism: Raja Parba and celebrations

festivals.name: Vaisakhi
festivals.description: Harvest celebrations coincide with the commemoration of the formation of the Khalsa, with gurdwara visits and community meals.
festivals.story: Vaisakhi brings together Punjab's harvest season and the Sikh commemoration of the formation of the Khalsa. Gurdwara visits, service and community meals are important, alongside local fairs and cultural programmes.
rituals: Gurdwara worship and kirtan
Community langar
Local fairs and processions
festivals.food: Langar is a communal meal grounded in service and equality; follow the volunteers' guidance.
festivals.dress: Cover your head and remove shoes where required in a gurdwara.
tips: Ask about visitor procedures at each religious venue.
Keep paths clear and ask before photographing worshippers.
places: Local Vaisakhi fair and religious celebrations.

festivals.name: Lohri
festivals.description: Families and communities gather around bonfires with folk songs and seasonal foods.
festivals.story: Lohri is a winter folk celebration strongly associated with Punjab and Punjabi communities elsewhere. An evening bonfire becomes a focus for gathering, singing and sharing seasonal treats. It expresses warmth and companionship during the cold season, and a family’s celebration may also mark a recent marriage or the arrival of a child. The character of the occasion depends on the hosts: a neighbourhood gathering, family party and organised cultural programme offer different experiences. A public programme is the simplest route for visitors who do not have a personal invitation.
rituals: Gathering around an evening bonfire
Folk songs and dancing in community celebrations
Sharing seasonal snacks among friends and neighbours
festivals.food: Peanuts, popcorn, revri and gajak are familiar Lohri treats. Sesame and nuts are common ingredients, so check allergens before sharing.
festivals.dress: Punjabi festive clothing may appear at organised events. Warm layers and practical footwear are useful for an outdoor evening.
tips: Keep loose clothing and children away from the fire and follow the organisers’ viewing boundaries.
Ask a local host about a public celebration; private family festivities are not open-access attractions.
places: City centre reference for Punjabi winter celebrations.

festivals.name: Gangaur
festivals.description: Women honour Gauri with rituals, decorated images and colourful processions.
festivals.story: Gangaur honours Gauri and is especially associated with women's devotional traditions in Rajasthan. Udaipur's Mewar Festival overlaps with these celebrations, giving the occasion a distinctive lakeside expression.
rituals: Worship of decorated images
Songs and processions
Local cultural programmes
festivals.food: Seek regional sweets and seasonal dishes; customs vary between families and towns.
festivals.dress: Colourful saris and regional dress are common in processions.
tips: Photograph respectfully without blocking processions.
Check the local route rather than assuming all cities share one programme.
places: Gangaur traditions around the old city and lakeside.
City processions subject to annual announcements.

festivals.name: Pushkar Fair
festivals.description: Around Kartik Purnima, pilgrims and visitors gather for a traditional fair, cultural events and lakeside rituals.
festivals.story: Pushkar Fair brings together livestock trading, pilgrimage and a public cultural fair in Rajasthan. The town’s lake, temples, markets and fairground create several overlapping experiences, so the most useful itinerary depends on whether you want to explore craft stalls, cultural performances or the religious setting. The trading activity and public entertainment do not necessarily peak on the same day. Pushkar’s sacred lake remains a place of worship during the festivities, and its ghats should be approached with the same care as a temple rather than as a photographic stage.
rituals: Livestock trading and fairground activity
Craft and textile stalls alongside cultural programmes
Pilgrimage and worship around Pushkar Lake
festivals.food: Explore the town’s vegetarian meals and sweet shops; fairground vendors offer snacks, but menus and hygiene arrangements differ.
festivals.dress: Comfortable walking clothes, sun protection and a layer for the evening work well; dress respectfully at the ghats.
tips: Check separate schedules for livestock activity and staged events before choosing your dates.
Ask before photographing traders, avoid obstructing animals and confirm any activity’s price before agreeing.
places: Town centre reference; lake ghats and fairground are different locations.

practical.duration: The national tourism listing gives 17–24 November for 2026. Livestock trading, cultural events and religious observances have distinct schedules.
practical.suggestedVisit: 2–3 days targeted to the activities you want to see, rather than the fair dates alone.
practical.cost: The tourism listing indicates no general festival ticket. Accommodation, organised experiences, rides and private viewing are separate; obtain itemised quotes before paying.
practical.booking: Confirm whether your dates match livestock activity or the pilgrimage programme. Check the exact location, transport and inclusions of any camp or package.

festivals.name: Losoong / Namsoong
festivals.description: Bhutia and Lepcha communities mark seasonal renewal through their distinct traditions and celebrations.
festivals.story: Losoong and Namsoong are closely associated seasonal celebrations in Sikkim, observed among Bhutia and Lepcha communities respectively. The period celebrates the harvest and includes family gatherings, while associated monastery programmes may feature ceremonial cham dances. The Government of Sikkim also notes traditional skills such as archery. These related observances should not erase differences between communities or be confused with Losar. A monastery’s dance programme can take place before the main family festival, making local confirmation especially important for visitors.
rituals: Family and community harvest celebrations
Cham dances at participating monasteries on their own schedules
Traditional games or archery where organised
festivals.food: Family meals reflect local traditions and preferences. Ask hosts about the menu; a regional dish available in Gangtok is not automatically a ceremonial food.
festivals.dress: Traditional Bhutia and Lepcha clothing may be seen at celebrations. Bring warm layers for winter outdoor viewing.
tips: Confirm the specific monastery’s programme rather than assuming all dances happen on the same day.
Remain outside the ritual performance area and follow monastery photography rules.
places: Planning base; confirm individual monastery and community venues.

festivals.name: Pongal
festivals.description: Families prepare freshly harvested rice in a ceremonial pot and honour the sun and cattle over several days.
festivals.story: Pongal expresses gratitude for the harvest, the sun and the animals that support farming. The festival unfolds through several days with different meanings, connecting Tamil households to the agricultural season.
rituals: Cooking freshly harvested rice until the pot overflows
Kolam designs at entrances
Mattu Pongal celebrations honouring cattle
festivals.food: Sweet sakkarai pongal is made with rice and jaggery; other dishes vary by household.
festivals.dress: Saris and veshtis are common festive clothing, though there is no universal visitor dress requirement.
tips: Ask permission before joining household or village ceremonies.
Treat animal-related events as separate programmes with their own access rules.
places: Tamil harvest traditions in and around the city.

practical.duration: A four-day harvest celebration; local and family observances differ.
practical.suggestedVisit: 1–2 days around a visitor-welcoming local programme, plus travel time.
practical.cost: No universal admission price applies to the cultural observance. Obtain quotes for organised experiences, transport and meals.
practical.booking: Ask a local organiser or host which activities welcome visitors. Family celebrations are not public events by default.

festivals.name: Tamil Puthandu
festivals.description: Temple visits, festive meals and decorated entrances welcome the Tamil New Year.
festivals.story: Puthandu marks the opening of the Tamil month of Chithirai and the beginning of the Tamil New Year. It is a time for family visits, greetings and renewal, with household decorations and worship forming part of many celebrations. Kolam designs at entrances welcome the occasion, while special meals bring generations together. Tamil communities around the world observe the festival, and households vary in how they combine religious and cultural customs. In Tamil Nadu, a temple visit can form part of the day, but each temple sets its own arrangements.
rituals: Kolam designs and decorated household entrances
New Year greetings and seeking elders’ blessings
Special worship and family meals
festivals.food: Mango pachadi is a well-known seasonal preparation; festive meals can also include rice, vegetable dishes, vadai and payasam. Household recipes differ.
festivals.dress: New or festive clothing is common. Follow the individual temple’s dress requirements if you plan to enter.
tips: Confirm temple opening and entry arrangements before setting out.
Do not confuse Tamil New Year with the separate multi-day Chithirai festival programme in Madurai.
places: City reference for Tamil New Year celebrations and temple visits.
sources: Ministry of Tourism: Tamil New Year

festivals.name: Bathukamma
festivals.description: Women arrange seasonal flowers in tiered stacks and gather around them to sing and celebrate.
festivals.story: Bathukamma celebrates seasonal flowers and the goddess through a distinctly Telangana tradition. Women arrange tiered floral stacks and gather around them to sing, before concluding celebrations at local water bodies.
rituals: Building layered flower arrangements
Singing in circles around the flowers
Local processions and immersion traditions
festivals.food: Shared offerings vary by day; maleeda is associated with celebrations.
festivals.dress: Festive saris and regional textiles are common; observe local guidance when joining a gathering.
tips: Ask a host before joining a community circle.
Use designated viewing areas and protect the flowers and waterside space.
places: Public gatherings and neighbourhood celebrations; venues vary each year.

photo.caption: Bathukamma celebration in Telangana. Historical photograph; the source’s recorded date does not establish the festival date.

festivals.name: Bonalu
festivals.description: Devotees offer decorated pots of food to the goddess Mahakali, accompanied by local processions.
festivals.story: Bonalu is a Telangana festival of devotion and thanksgiving to Mahakali. In Hyderabad, Secunderabad and other communities, women carry decorated pots containing a prepared food offering to the goddess. The name is associated with the meal offered, and the procession combines devotion with strong neighbourhood participation. Celebrations take place through the month of Ashadam, with different temples and localities following their own schedules. A visitor should therefore choose a particular temple programme rather than assume there is one citywide festival day.
rituals: Preparing and carrying the bonam offering in decorated pots
Temple worship dedicated to Mahakali
Neighbourhood processions and accompanying music
festivals.food: The bonam is a sacred food offering; descriptions include cooked rice, jaggery and curd. Preparations vary, and offerings are not general visitor refreshments.
festivals.dress: Women carrying offerings often wear festive traditional attire. Visitors should dress respectfully and leave room for worshippers.
tips: Check the schedule for the particular Hyderabad or Secunderabad temple you wish to visit.
Avoid standing in the procession’s path or interrupting someone carrying an offering for a photograph.
places: City reference; temple celebrations occur at multiple locations.

festivals.name: Kharchi Puja
festivals.description: The Fourteen Gods are honoured through rituals and a public fair at the Chaturdasha Devata temple.
festivals.story: Kharchi Puja is one of Tripura’s major religious festivals, centred on the Fourteen Gods temple at Old Agartala. Its traditions connect the state’s historic royal worship with a much wider gathering of devotees and visitors. Ceremonies and a surrounding fair bring different communities together over several days. For a visitor, the temple observance and the public fair are related but distinct spaces: worshippers take priority around sacred objects and ritual routes. The lunar calendar and local organisers determine the programme each year.
rituals: Worship associated with the fourteen deities
Ceremonial activities led by the temple’s religious authorities
A public fair and community gathering around the festival
festivals.food: Sweets and other offerings have devotional roles. Food sold at the fair is a separate visitor choice; ask about ingredients and serving arrangements.
festivals.dress: Respectful clothing suitable for temple surroundings is appropriate. Follow instructions about footwear and restricted areas.
tips: Confirm the current temple and fair timetable before travelling from central Agartala.
Ask before photographing rituals and allow extra time for queues near the shrine.
places: Approximate locality near the Fourteen Gods temple; confirm the entrance locally.
sources: Tripura Information and Cultural Affairs: Kharchi Festival

festivals.name: Garia Puja
festivals.description: Traditional prayers and community celebrations seek wellbeing and a prosperous agricultural season.
festivals.story: Garia Puja is a spring observance among indigenous communities of Tripura, centred on prayers for well-being and prosperity. Ritual offerings and community celebration are important, but practices belong to particular communities and hosts rather than to a single statewide tourist performance. The Department of Information and Cultural Affairs documents a range of ritual ingredients, showing how material offerings form part of the observance. Visitors should seek a public programme or an invitation from a local host who can explain the significance of what is taking place.
rituals: Community worship and offerings associated with Garia
Gatherings that express hopes for prosperity and welfare
Music and dance where included in local cultural programmes
festivals.food: Ritual offerings can include rice, eggs and other items, according to local custom. They should not be treated as a standard visitor meal.
festivals.dress: Community-specific woven dress may feature in celebrations. Ask before wearing ceremonial garments or borrowing accessories.
tips: Use a local cultural host to identify a gathering that welcomes visitors.
Do not handle ritual objects or offerings; ask the host about any restrictions before taking photographs.
places: Planning base for community-led events; not a guaranteed ritual venue.
sources: Tripura Information and Cultural Affairs: Garia Puja

festivals.name: Holi
festivals.description: The Braj region’s distinctive celebrations combine devotional singing and colourful traditions over several days.
festivals.story: Holi celebrates spring through colour, gathering and stories of renewal. In the Braj region, celebrations are connected with Krishna traditions. Different towns hold distinct events on different days around the main festival.
rituals: Holika Dahan bonfires in many communities
Colour celebrations
Devotional singing and regional performances
festivals.food: Gujiya is a familiar festive sweet in northern India; local menus vary.
festivals.dress: Choose comfortable clothes that can be stained. Clothing is not consent to participate.
tips: Ask before applying colour or photographing participants.
Select an organised event if you prefer clear boundaries and facilities.
places: Temple programmes require their own date and access checks.

practical.duration: Holika Dahan is observed on the eve of the colour celebration. Braj and other local programmes can extend beyond these two occasions.
practical.suggestedVisit: 2–3 days in one base; allow extra days only for specifically dated regional events.
practical.cost: Budget separately for a hosted colour event, transport, meals and clothing you can stain. Check inclusions before paying; a tour price is not a public festival entry fee.
practical.booking: Choose a named venue or host and confirm its date, admission policy and facilities. Book a specific local programme rather than assuming every Braj town celebrates on the same day.

festivals.name: Dev Deepawali
festivals.description: On Kartik Purnima, thousands of lamps illuminate the Ganges ghats in a spectacular riverside celebration.
festivals.story: Dev Deepawali transforms Varanasi’s riverfront with rows of lamps on Kartik Purnima. It is a separate observance from the main Diwali night, with worship, prayers and cultural activity focused on the Ganga and its ghats. The illuminated steps are visually striking, but they remain working public and sacred spaces. A riverside walk, a fixed viewing point and a boat trip offer very different experiences; choose one that suits your group’s mobility and comfort with crowds. The exact event programme and access arrangements change by edition.
rituals: Lighting lamps along the ghats
Prayers and riverfront religious observances
Cultural music and performances where scheduled
festivals.food: Varanasi’s local snacks and sweets can be explored away from the busiest viewing areas. Festival offerings should be handled only as directed by organisers.
festivals.dress: Wear comfortable shoes with grip for steps and respectful clothing around worship areas. Carry a light evening layer.
tips: Identify your return route before the ghats become crowded.
For boat viewing, confirm boarding location, capacity and life-jacket provision directly with the operator.
places: City reference; choose and confirm a particular ghat or boarding point.

festivals.name: Harela
festivals.description: Seedlings grown in the days before the festival symbolise greenery, prosperity and the agricultural season.
festivals.story: Harela celebrates greenery and the close relationship between people and the agricultural landscape of Uttarakhand. The monsoon observance is especially associated with Kumaon, while contemporary celebrations across the state include tree planting and environmental activities. The festival offers a useful introduction to living local traditions beyond the better-known pilgrimage routes. A household ceremony, village gathering and organised plantation event may each emphasise different aspects. Visitors interested in joining should choose a publicly announced activity and learn from the organisers about its local meaning.
rituals: Seasonal celebrations connected with greenery and agriculture
Family or community observances according to local custom
Tree-planting programmes organised by community and public bodies
festivals.food: Meals depend on the household or event. Try regional Kumaoni food through a local host, without assuming that one dish defines every Harela celebration.
festivals.dress: Comfortable clothing suitable for outdoor activity is useful. For planting programmes, use footwear that can cope with mud.
tips: Check the local programme and weather before travelling to an outdoor activity.
Join planting only through organisers who select appropriate species and arrange ongoing care.
places: Kumaon town reference; confirm a public local programme.

festivals.name: Phool Dei
festivals.description: Children place flowers at doorsteps to welcome spring and offer blessings for the household.
festivals.story: Phool Dei welcomes spring in Uttarakhand through a gentle tradition closely associated with children. Flowers are placed at household thresholds with wishes for happiness and prosperity, linking neighbourhood life with the changing season. Cultural organisations also arrange public celebrations to help younger generations learn the songs and customs. It is principally a community practice rather than a large destination festival. A host-led visit offers a better understanding than searching for a single central venue, and visitors should respect the privacy of homes and participating families.
rituals: Children placing flowers at thresholds
Good wishes and seasonal songs
Community activities that pass traditions between generations
festivals.food: Households may share small treats with participating children; offerings and recipes vary. Ask parents before giving children any food.
festivals.dress: Everyday or locally chosen festive dress is appropriate; practical footwear helps when moving between homes.
tips: Seek a public cultural event or a host’s invitation rather than following children into private homes.
Ask parental permission before photographing children and use flowers obtained without damaging wild plants.
places: Town reference for local spring traditions; public venues vary.

festivals.name: Durga Puja
festivals.description: Neighbourhoods become open-air galleries of elaborate pandals and Durga idols. Dhak drums, dhunuchi dance and shared bhog bring people together in a celebration of creativity and devotion.
festivals.story: Durga Puja honours the goddess Durga and her victory over Mahishasura. In Bengal, it is also imagined as a daughter's homecoming. Kolkata's neighbourhood pandals make the celebration a meeting of public art, craftsmanship and worship.
rituals: Pandal visits and viewing crafted idols
Dhak drumming, prayers and dhunuchi dance
Immersion processions at the close of the observance
festivals.food: Shared bhog often includes khichuri; sweets and family meals are part of the wider celebrations.
festivals.dress: Saris, kurtas and everyday festive clothing; red-and-white combinations are a familiar sight, not a visitor requirement.
tips: Ask before photographing worship or individuals.
Visit earlier in the day for a gentler introduction; evening queues can be long.
places: Neighbourhood pandals and public art; individual opening times vary.

practical.duration: Main celebrations peak over five days, from Sasthi to Dashami.
practical.suggestedVisit: 2–3 days to explore a few Kolkata neighbourhoods at an unhurried pace.
practical.cost: No single festival-wide price is verified here. Budget separately for local travel, meals and any guided tours or special-access offers.
practical.booking: Choose your pandal areas first, then arrange accommodation and transport. Check access with each organiser; do not assume a tour includes priority entry.

festivals.name: Kali Puja
festivals.description: Homes and temples honour Goddess Kali with lamps, offerings and evening worship around the new moon.
festivals.story: Kali Puja honours the goddess Kali and is particularly prominent in West Bengal. Temples, household shrines and neighbourhood pandals each create their own setting for worship, often with elaborate images and lighting. The observance falls around the autumn new moon associated with Diwali, but its devotional focus is distinct. Kolkata offers both major temple traditions and community celebrations; a carefully chosen neighbourhood route is more practical than trying to see everything in one night. Ritual timing and visitor access should be checked with each venue.
rituals: Worship of Kali at temples and household or community shrines
Decorated pandals and goddess images
Evening lighting and neighbourhood gatherings
festivals.food: Prasad and meals vary widely by temple and community. Ask organisers what is available and avoid assuming that every venue serves the same offerings.
festivals.dress: Festive clothing is common, while visitors should choose respectful dress and comfortable shoes for queues and walking.
tips: Check whether photography is permitted inside a temple or pandal.
Keep routes short enough for your group, and arrange a meeting point away from the busiest entrance.
places: City reference; temple and neighbourhood pandal locations differ.

festivals.name: Poila Boishakh
festivals.description: New account books, cultural programmes and generous Bengali meals mark the start of the Bengali year.
festivals.story: Poila Boishakh marks the beginning of the Bengali calendar year. In West Bengal, it brings together family meals, new clothes, greetings and cultural programmes. Some businesses observe Halkhata, the symbolic opening of a new accounts ledger, often welcoming customers with sweets. Music, neighbourhood activity and household traditions give the occasion a character that extends beyond a single religious setting. Kolkata is a useful base, though celebrations also take place across Bengali communities. Follow the local calendar rather than assuming every country or community observes an identical date.
rituals: New Year greetings and family gatherings
Halkhata customs among participating businesses
Music, cultural programmes and household alpana designs
festivals.food: Bengali sweets and festive meals are prominent, but menus vary by household and restaurant. Book a special restaurant meal directly if that is your preferred experience.
festivals.dress: Saris, kurtas and other new festive clothing are common choices; there is no required visitor costume.
tips: Choose an announced cultural programme for public participation.
Ask a shopkeeper before photographing a Halkhata ceremony; it is a business and devotional custom, not a staged attraction.
places: City reference for Bengali New Year cultural programmes.
